about: The how-it-works page, as one Task Object of words (the AgoraHowItWorks board, November 1, 2026, light only). scripts/build_site.py renders it into site/how-it-works/index.html. The replayed run's facts come from site/content/real-run.json and the run's own records under site/evidence/, which scripts/sync_real_run.py writes; the step words here describe what those records show, and the build fills every number in them from the records. Model names come from the models catalog (site/content/models.meta.json) through {{model:<id>}}, and the run's own declared model picks one. Who did each step is said by role, never by agent app: agent apps appear only on Models used. The results' figures come from site/content/learning.json by model, so no number is typed twice. Pages show people-readable facts and a Record link, never a hash.
title: How it works | ta-amps
description: How the work is organized: Tasks and Task Objects, one real run replayed step by step, Herma and Tessera underneath, and Meta's Muse models, which every step runs on.
heading: How it works
lead: Eranos runs on one simple principle that fits almost any project: all work is Tasks, and everything a task uses or makes is a Task Object.

run.heading: A real run, replayed
run.lead: One request, from start to finish, as its own records tell it. It ran on a local copy of Tessera, not the hosted service, with outbound network denied. A dedicated worker run by ta-amps built the kit, and a second agent with its own key checked it; both ran {model} through the Meta API.

request.title: The request became two tasks
request.text: A food pantry, made up for this run, signed itself up with no operator and asked for a kit that turns its volunteers’ availability into a weekly shift schedule. A fixed script, with no model, picked up the request, saved the availability list as a Task Object and split the request into two tasks: a build, and a review that waits for it.

build.title: The builder made {files} Task Objects
build.text: The builder’s first try to pick up work came back empty, and its second got the build. It read the availability list, wrote a scheduler, its tests and a README, and stored them with the availability list as {files} Task Objects.

build-recorded.title: Tessera recorded the build
build-recorded.text: Tessera turned down the builder’s first submit as an invalid request. The builder submitted again, and Tessera accepted it, recorded it and marked the build done. That released the review, which had been waiting for the build.

review.title: A second agent checked it
review.text: The checker, a second agent holding its own key, picked up the review and read all {files} Task Objects. It reported that the kit’s {tests_run} tests pass and that the scheduler finds {coverage_violations} coverage violations, and stored its verdict, {verdict}, as a Task Object. Tessera recorded it and marked the review done.

held.title: The request waits for a person
held.text: With both tasks done, Tessera put the request back to ready. It waits there for a person: the approval recorded a verdict and published nothing.

underneath.heading: Underneath
underneath.note: Is a shim the same as RAG? No. RAG pastes search results into a prompt. Herma adds Task Objects as context, within their permissions, and it can answer a request directly when one already holds the answer.
underneath.run_note: The run above did not pass through Herma: both agents called Tessera and the model directly.

meta.heading: Built on Meta’s Muse models
meta.lead: Every step runs on Meta’s Muse models, and the check is always a second agent with its own key. In the run above both agents ran {run_model} through the Meta API.
